question:
Patient note:
A previously healthy 31-year-old man who works as a freelance videographer and spends most weekends trail-running was brought to the hospital by advanced life-support ambulance after collapsing in the parking lot outside his apartment complex roughly forty minutes before arrival. Neighbors told paramedics he had returned the night before from a three-day desert music festival where daytime temperatures exceeded 40 °C and reported via text that he had been “puking and coughing” since the ride home. They observed that he had voided only once overnight, had drunk mainly energy drinks, and had taken no over-the-counter medications aside from two acetaminophen tablets. He has never smoked, uses alcohol sparingly, denies recreational drug use, has no known allergies, and his most recent employment physical two years earlier was normal. He has never required hospitalization, takes no prescription medications, and has no history of chronic liver, lung, kidney, hematologic, or endocrine disease. In the field he was found seated against a curb, flushed, febrile to touch, breathing rapidly but speaking in full sentences; fingertip pulse oximetry on ambient air read 82 %, prompting application of a high-flow face mask that respiratory therapy later measured at 52 % inspired oxygen. No intravenous fluids, anti-emetics, bronchodilators, vasopressors, or antimicrobial agents were started during the twelve-minute transport. On entry to the resuscitation bay—and prior to any hospital intervention—the trauma nurse documented a tympanic temperature of 39.1 °C, a regular tachycardic pulse of 117 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 27 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, and non-invasive blood pressure of 119/64 mm Hg confirmed by a repeat cuff on the opposite arm. The patient was sitting upright, sweating profusely, conversing but intermittently confused about the exact calendar date, opened his eyes spontaneously, and obeyed two-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 14 without exposure to ethanol or sedatives. Skin was hot and dry with salt crystals visible along the forehead; mucous membranes were tacky, capillary refill was just under three seconds, and peripheral pulses were bounding. Neck veins were flat at 30°, heart sounds revealed a rapid S1 and single S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally at the bases with scattered inspiratory crackles but no wheezes; percussion was mildly dull posteriorly. The abdomen was scaphoid, mildly tender in the epigastrium with voluntary guarding but no rebound, and bowel sounds were hyperactive. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness and no peripheral edema. Neurologic examination showed brisk reflexes, no focal deficits, and intact coordination of finger-nose testing. A radial arterial sample drawn eight minutes after stretcher placement—while he remained on the same 52 % oxygen mask—revealed a pH of 7.54; the respiratory therapist calculated an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient of 274 mm Hg, indicating substantial impairment of gas transfer. Point-of-care chemistry reported serum sodium 157 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L, glucose 108 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.22 mg/dL, the latter very close to a documented baseline of 1.1 mg/dL from a sports physical six months prior. A complete blood count showed white blood cell count 18 500 / mm³ with 88 % neutrophils, hematocrit 36 %, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, and platelets 264 000 / µL. Venous lactate measured 2.1 mmol/L. End-tidal CO₂ on the monitor was 22 mm Hg, consistent with the marked alkalemia. Portable chest radiography obtained before antibiotics or intravenous fluids demonstrated patchy, ill-defined opacities in both lower lobes without pleural effusion or cardiomegaly. Focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a hyperdynamic left ventricle and a small, collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.3 cm in expiration, suggesting intravascular volume depletion rather than cardiogenic pulmonary edema. No pericardial effusion was visualized. Electrocardiography performed concurrently displayed sinus tachycardia at 118 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no ischemic changes. A bladder scan showed less than 50 mL of urine, and the Foley inserted immediately afterward produced only 20 mL of concentrated amber fluid over the first fifteen minutes. No crystalloids, antipyretics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, vasopressors, or antimicrobial agents had been initiated at the moment the critical care team accepted him for admission with presumptive diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by hypernatremic dehydration and respiratory alkalosis; therefore, the values of temperature 39.1 °C, heart rate 117 beats/min, respiratory rate 27 breaths/min, blood pressure 119/64 mm Hg, arterial pH 7.54, sodium 157 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 1.22 mg/dL, hematocrit 36 %, white blood cell count 18 500 / mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 52 %, and alveolar-arterial gradient 274 mm Hg accurately represent his untreated physiologic state at the time of ICU admission.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II sums 12 acute physiology components, age points, and chronic health points. Using the supplied ICU admission measurements:
- Temperature 39.1 °C (39.0–40.9) → 3.
- Mean arterial pressure = (119 + 2 × 64)/3 ≈ 82 mm Hg (70–109) → 0.
- Heart rate 117/min (110–139) → 2.
- Respiratory rate 27/min (25–34) → 1.
- Oxygenation: FiO₂ 0.52 is ≥0.50, so use the A–a gradient. A gradient of 274 mm Hg (200–349) → 2.
- Arterial pH 7.54 (7.50–7.59) → 1.
- Sodium 157 mmol/L (155–159) → 2.
- Potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.4) → 0.
- Creatinine 1.22 mg/dL (0.6–1.4) → 0.
- Hematocrit 36% (30–45.9%) → 0.
- WBC 18.5 × 10³/mm³ (15–19.9) → 1.
- Neurologic points = 15 − GCS = 15 − 14 = 1.
Acute physiology subtotal = 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 13. Age 31 (<45) → 0; no severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise → 0. Total = 13 + 0 + 0 = 13.
Final answer: 13
